stem: How can specialized wearable consumer devices, such as smartwatches, support individuals with active seizure disorders?

options.text: By measuring blood oxygen saturation to predict the onset of a seizure.
options.shortLabel: Blood oxygen monitoring to predict seizures
options.rationale: Pulse oximetry measures blood oxygen; it does not predict when a seizure will begin.

options.text: By delivering a mild electrical pulse through the wrist sensor pad to interrupt seizure activity.
options.rationale: Consumer smartwatches do not deliver therapeutic electrical stimulation; implanted devices such as vagus nerve stimulators are separate treatments.

options.text: By placing a call to emergency services whenever the wearer's heart rate rises.
options.shortLabel: Calls emergency services on heart rate rise
options.rationale: Alerts go to designated contacts and are triggered by detected seizure activity, not by heart rate alone.

options.text: By detecting abnormal convulsive motion patterns and transmitting automated emergency alerts.
options.shortLabel: Detect convulsive motion and send alerts
options.rationale: Smartwatches and dedicated seizure monitors use onboard motion sensors and algorithms to recognize repetitive convulsive patterns, such as tonic-clonic seizures, and send alert notifications with location details to caregivers.

explanation: Specialized wearable applications and smart monitors support individuals with seizure disorders by using onboard motion sensors (accelerometers) and physiological sensors to detect the repetitive, convulsive movements typical of generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Upon detection, the device initiates an automated alert containing the wearer's real-time GPS coordinates to designated emergency contacts or caregivers.
